## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Missing Data and Inferences about School Summaries
• Suboptimal participation rates on the RICAS have led to concerns about the reporting
of summary statistics (e.g., percent proficient, median SGP, …) for schools.
• How would summary statistics at the school look if all (or at least 95%) of the
students participated.
• Related to this: Is there a participation rate below which the summary statistics
cannot be trusted to be representative of all students?
• An answer to either question clearly rests on an understanding of the missing data.
• Clearly, if the data are missing completely at random, then even a small percentage of
student testing yields an unbiased estimate of the entire school.
• Thus, an answer to the 2nd question is not likely to yield a single number without a
uniform mechanism causing missingness across all schools.
• However, number that works in most cases might be possible.

Multiple Imputation Approaches to Missing RICAS Data 2</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Missing Data and Inferences about School Summaries
• The simplest brute force approach to understanding what impact
missing data could have is presented by in the paper where:
• Missing data are replaced with the LOSS/LOT (lowest obtainable scale score/
lowest obtainable theta)
• Missing data re replaced with the HOSS/HOT (highest obtainable scale score/
highest obtainable theta)
• Summary statistics for each school can be calculated based upon the
worst-case and best-case scenario, respectively.
• Not surprisingly, this approach leads to substantial changes in
observed values with even modest missing data.
Multiple Imputation Approaches to Missing RICAS Data 3</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Multiple Imputation
• A more sophisticated approach is to utilize modern approaches to
characterizing and imputing missing data.
• Multiple imputation is a widely used technique to infer missing data,
especially in longitudinal studies.
• NOTE: Our goal for these techniques is NOT to replace the observed
data with a “better” estimate.
• The goal is to calculate the better estimate and its standard error/
confidence band. If the observed score lies outside of this confidence
band (at a designated significance level), then the missing data is
believed to be a biased estimate.
Multiple Imputation Approaches to Missing RICAS Data 4</div>
```
